name: Sì Sè Pái
description: Sì Sè Pái (Four Color Cards or Si Se Pai) is a Chinese card game similar to Rummy or Mahjong. It uses a deck of 112 cards divided into 4 colors (Red, Green, Yellow, White), featuring Chinese Chess pieces (General, Advisor, Elephant, etc.). The goal is to meld cards into sets (Commanders/Generals can be melded singly, Pairs, Triplets/Pongs, Quads/Kongs) to reach an odd number of points (usually 21 cards total).
deck: 112 cards (4 Suits x 7 Ranks x 4 Copies per Card).

history.origins: The game has a long history in southern China and is similar to Chinese draw-and-discard games played since the 18th century. The deck originated in the 19th century based on Xiangqi (Chinese chess) pieces. Stewart Culin noted these chess-derived cards were peculiar to Fujian and Guangdong; Karl Himly confirmed they were specific to Fujian. Chess cards are more recent than money-suited and domino cards. The cards were often used for gambling and may have appeared after the 1740 Qing ban on playing cards.
timeline: Today: Popular in Vietnam (Tu Sac) and Taiwan.
history.cultural: Played in tea houses and family gatherings.

setup.deck: 112 cards: four color suits (green, white, yellow, red), 28 cards per suit, each with the seven Xiangqi piece ranks and four copies per card; some sets include optional jokers.
setup.dealing: Deal 20 cards to non-dealers, 21 to dealer.

rules.objective: Go out (Hu) by melding all of your cards into valid sets (single General, pairs, Pongs, Kongs) so that your total point value is an odd number; the first player to do so wins the hand.
rules.gameplay: Each turn a player draws one card from the stock or the top of the discard pile, may lay down melds (single General, pairs, triplets/Pongs, quads/Kongs), then discards one card. The first to go out (Hu) by melding all cards with an odd point total wins the hand. Point system uses piece values; Generals score high.
keyRules: Draw one from stock or top discard, then optionally meld, then discard one.
Melds: single General, pairs, triplets (Pongs), quads (Kongs).
Go out (Hu) when all cards are melded and total points are odd (e.g. 21).

strategy.basic: Keep pairs. Pairs become Pongs easily. Don't break up Chows unless necessary. Watch discards to know what's safe.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Sacrifice': Discarding a dangerous card early to avoid a huge penalty later. If you have 3 Generals, keep them for a Pong.
strategy.advanced: Defensive Discarding: Don't feed the next player. If they need Green Advisors, hold them.
